notes.front: What is the legislative branch?
notes.back: The branch that makes federal laws; also called Congress.
notes.explanation: It is one of the three branches taught in the previous topic, now covered in detail.
notes.example: Like a town council whose only job is writing the town's rules.

notes.front: What is Congress?
notes.back: The legislative branch, made of the Senate and the House of Representatives.
notes.explanation: “Congress” and “legislative branch” name the same thing; Congress has two parts, taught next.
notes.example: Example: Congress has two groups, the Senate and the House. Together they make laws.

notes.front: What is the Senate?
notes.back: The part of Congress with 100 senators, two from each state.
notes.explanation: It is one of Congress's two chambers, giving every state equal weight regardless of population.
notes.example: Like an upper chamber where every member state sends exactly two delegates.

notes.front: What is a senator?
notes.back: A member of the Senate; represents all the people of a state; elected for six years.
notes.explanation: A senator's district is an entire state, unlike a representative's smaller district (taught next).
notes.example: Like a state's two seats on a national council, each held for a six-year term.

notes.front: What is the House of Representatives?
notes.back: The part of Congress with 435 voting members; states with more people have more representatives.
notes.explanation: It is Congress's other chamber, giving more populous states a bigger voice than the Senate does.
notes.example: Like a lower chamber where seats are handed out by each state's population.

notes.front: What is a representative?
notes.back: A member of the House, elected by a congressional district every two years.
notes.explanation: Unlike a senator, a representative's district is smaller than a whole state.
notes.example: Like one local council seat, elected from just one part of a state.

notes.front: What is a congressional district?
notes.back: An area of a state that elects one representative.
notes.explanation: It is the unit a representative is elected from, smaller than the state a senator represents.
notes.example: Like a ward inside a city, each ward sending one member to the city council.

notes.front: What was the Great Compromise?
notes.back: The 1787 agreement, also called the Connecticut Compromise, giving equal representation in the Senate and representation by population in the House.
notes.explanation: It is why the Senate and House use two different ways of counting seats.
notes.source: Senate.gov, Equal State Representation; study guide p.18
notes.example: Small states wanted equal seats; big states wanted seats by population. They agreed: equal seats in the Senate, seats by population in the House.

notes.front: What is the Speaker of the House?
notes.back: The leader of the House of Representatives; next in the line of succession after the Vice President.
notes.explanation: The office is fixed; only who currently holds it changes with elections (a later card covers that).
notes.source: Study guide p.20, p.27; test updates
notes.example: If the President and Vice President both cannot serve, the Speaker becomes President.

notes.front: What is a nonvoting delegate?
notes.back: Territories may have a nonvoting Delegate or Resident Commissioner in the House instead of a voting representative.
notes.explanation: They can speak in the House but cannot vote on laws.
notes.example: Like a non-voting observer seat at a council table, able to speak but not to cast the deciding vote.

notes.front: What is a bill?
notes.back: A proposal for a new law.
notes.explanation: It is what Congress actually writes and votes on before anything becomes law.
notes.source: Study guide p.22; USA.gov, how laws are made
notes.example: Like a draft policy submitted for a vote, before it is adopted.

notes.front: What is a (federal) law?
notes.back: A rule that people must follow; a federal law is a rule that everyone in the United States must follow.
notes.explanation: A bill becomes a law only once it passes the steps taught in this topic and the next.
notes.example: Like a town rule that, once passed, everyone in the town must follow.

notes.front: What is a majority?
notes.back: More than half of those voting.
notes.explanation: Congress uses it as the ordinary threshold for passing a bill.
notes.example: Like a vote that passes once it gets more than half of the votes cast.

notes.front: What is the federal budget, as a power of Congress?
notes.back: Making the federal budget is one power of Congress.
notes.explanation: It is one of the listed accepted answers to “name one power of Congress.”
notes.example: Like a family deciding how much of its money to spend on rent, food and school each year.

notes.front: What power does the Constitution give Congress over war?
notes.back: The Constitution gives Congress the power “To declare War.”
notes.explanation: It is Congress's power, distinct from the President's Commander-in-Chief role taught in the next topic.
notes.source: Constitution Art. I, sec. 8; study guide p.13, p.64
notes.example: Example: in 1941 Congress voted to declare war on Japan.

notes.front: Name the three branches of government?
notes.explanation: USCIS also accepts naming them by institution: Congress, president, and the courts. Other accepted answers: Congress, president, and the courts.

notes.front: The President of the United States is in charge of which branch of government?
notes.explanation: The executive branch itself is covered in the next topic; here it just contrasts with Congress.

notes.front: What part of the federal government writes laws?
notes.explanation: USCIS also accepts “legislature” and “legislative branch” as the same answer. Other accepted answers: (U.S. or national) legislature; Legislative branch.

notes.front: What are the two parts of the U.S. Congress?
notes.explanation: Congress has two parts, and you must name both.

notes.front: Name one power of the U.S. Congress?
notes.explanation: USCIS also accepts declaring war or making the federal budget. One of the 20 questions for 65/20 applicants. (65/20) Other accepted answers: Declares war; Makes the federal budget.

notes.front: How many U.S. senators are there?
notes.explanation: 100 comes from 2 senators times 50 states.

notes.front: How long is a term for a U.S. senator?
notes.explanation: This is longer than a representative's term, taught later in this topic.

notes.front: Who is one of your state's U.S. senators now?
notes.back: Answers vary by state. Find your two senators at senate.gov before your interview.
notes.explanation: D.C. residents and residents of U.S. territories should answer that they have no U.S. senators.

notes.front: How many voting members are in the House of Representatives?
notes.explanation: The number stays 435; each state's share changes with population.

notes.front: How long is a term for a member of the House of Representatives?
notes.explanation: This is shorter than a senator's six-year term, on purpose (next card).

notes.front: Why do U.S. representatives serve shorter terms than U.S. senators?
notes.back: To more closely follow public opinion.
notes.explanation: Frequent elections keep the House more responsive to recent shifts in opinion.

notes.front: How many senators does each state have?
notes.explanation: Every state gets the same number regardless of its population.

notes.front: Why does each state have two senators?
notes.explanation: USCIS also accepts naming the Great Compromise directly. Other accepted answers: The Great Compromise (Connecticut Compromise).

notes.front: Name your U.S. representative?
notes.back: Answers vary by state. Find yours at house.gov (enter your home postal code).
notes.explanation: Residents of territories with a nonvoting Delegate or Resident Commissioner may name that person instead. Also acceptable is any statement that the territory has no (voting) representatives in Congress.

notes.front: What is the name of the Speaker of the House of Representatives now?
notes.explanation: One of the 20 questions for 65/20 applicants; check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates before an interview. (65/20) Other accepted answers: Johnson; James Michael Johnson.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · verify at uscis.gov (as of USCIS's 09/18/2025 update)

notes.front: Who does a U.S. senator represent?
notes.explanation: USCIS also accepts “people of their state,” a wider phrasing. Other accepted answers: People of their state.

notes.front: Who elects U.S. senators?
notes.explanation: This is the only listed accepted answer.

notes.front: Who does a member of the House of Representatives represent?
notes.explanation: USCIS accepts several near-identical phrasings, citizen- or people-based, district- or not. Other accepted answers: Citizens in their district; People from their (congressional) district; People in their district.

notes.front: Who elects members of the House of Representatives?
notes.explanation: This is the only listed accepted answer.

notes.front: Some states have more representatives than other states. Why?
notes.explanation: USCIS also accepts “they have more people” as the same idea in plainer words. Other accepted answers: (Because) they have more people; (Because) some states have more people.

notes.front: How many votes make a majority in the House, and in the Senate?
notes.back: 218 in the House (of 435); 51 in the Senate (of 100), or a majority of those voting and present.
notes.explanation: These are simply more than half of each chamber's full membership.

notes.front: What is the minimum age to serve in the House, and in the Senate?
notes.back: 25 for the House; 30 for the Senate.
notes.explanation: Senators must be older.

notes.front: How many voting House seats do California and Wyoming each have, as an example of population-based seats?
notes.back: California 52; Wyoming 1 (figures from the study guide; these numbers can change).
notes.explanation: This is a concrete example of why some states have more representatives than others.

notes.front: Which branch of the federal government makes laws?
notes.explanation: It is one of the three branches, distinct from the branch that enforces or reviews laws.

notes.front: What is the name for the federal body made up of the Senate and House together?
notes.explanation: Congress is the institution; “legislative branch” is its role.

notes.front: Which chamber of Congress gives every state exactly two seats?
notes.explanation: It contrasts with the House, whose seats are set by population.

notes.front: A person represents their whole state in Congress for a six-year term. What is their title?
notes.explanation: The six-year term and statewide district identify the office.

notes.front: Which chamber of Congress has 435 voting seats split by state population?
notes.explanation: It contrasts with the Senate, where every state gets exactly two seats.

notes.front: A person represents one part of their state in Congress for a two-year term. What is their title?
notes.explanation: The two-year term and district-sized constituency identify the office.

notes.front: What is the name for the area within a state that elects one member of the House?
notes.explanation: It is smaller than a state, unlike the area a senator represents.

notes.front: Why does the Senate use equal representation while the House uses representation by population?
notes.back: The Great Compromise, at the 1787 Convention, settled the two chambers on different rules.
notes.explanation: It resolved the fight between large and small states over how seats should be counted.

notes.front: Which House office is next in the line of succession after the Vice President?
notes.explanation: The office, not the current officeholder, is what this card tests.

notes.front: A new law starts as an idea written down for Congress to vote on. What is it called?
notes.explanation: A bill is only a proposal until it passes the steps a law requires.

notes.front: Once passed, what must everyone in the United States follow?
notes.explanation: This is the end result of a bill successfully passing Congress and being signed.

notes.front: A bill gets 220 of 435 House votes in favour. Has it passed the House?
notes.back: Yes: 220 is more than half of 435, a majority.
notes.explanation: 220 clears the simple-majority threshold of 218.

notes.front: Which branch of government holds the constitutional power to declare war?
notes.explanation: This is Congress's own power, separate from the President's role as Commander in Chief.

notes.front: What is the difference between a senator and a representative?
notes.back: Senator: 100 total, 2 per state, 6-year term, represents a whole state. Representative: 435 total, by population, 2-year term, represents a district.
notes.explanation: Mixing these up is a common trap because both sit in Congress but follow opposite rules for how seats are assigned.
notes.contrast: The Great Compromise is why the Senate counts states equally while the House counts people.
